headline: Ran the East Wall on a Hunch — Six Yellowfin and Our First White Marlin of the Year
subhead: A warm-water eddy tucked against the Wilmington's edge turned a coin-flip troll into the best day we've had since June.
body_markdown:
Monday morning I had two options on the plotter and about ninety minutes to decide between them: run to the Baltimore and gamble on a temp break nobody had confirmed, or make the shorter run to the Wilmington's east wall where satellite showed a warm eddy pinched up tight against the canyon edge. I picked the Wilmington. Fuel math said it was the smarter play even if the fish weren't there — shorter run, more time on the trolley if we had to grind for bites. Turned out we didn't have to grind much.

We set up around 38°47'N, 72°38'W, working the spur where the bottom breaks from 600 fathoms up onto the 100-fathom curve, and the color change was obvious by 7 a.m. — that green-to-blue seam you can see without even looking at the water temp gauge. We had a nine-line spread out, naked ballyhoo in the shotgun and long riggers, Green Machines and a small Ilander in the pattern, and it didn't take twenty minutes before the left short corner buried. Yellowfin, maybe 55 pounds, clean fish, fat with squid. We picked at that same stretch of edge for four hours and boxed six yellowfin between 45 and 68 pounds, plus a mahi that came up on a teaser and wouldn't leave the spread alone until we stuck a naked ballyhoo in front of it.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the new moon tide would concentrate bait tight against the shelf break, and that's exactly what we found. The current was ripping harder than normal for mid-July, and everywhere that eddy pinched down against the canyon wall, we found bait balls stacked thick on the sounder, 180 to 240 feet down, with tuna working underneath them. That's not luck. That's the moon doing what the moon does this time of year — squeezing bait into a smaller window and making the fish easier to find, if you're willing to run to where the edge is actually working instead of where it worked last week.

Wednesday we switched gears entirely. Ran back out to the same general area but instead of trolling, we anchored up on the warm side of that break around dusk and started chunking butterfish over the transom. This is where the Wilmington earns its reputation — once that sun drops and you've got a slick of oily chunks drifting back into dark water, the yellowfin come up out of the depths and feed right under the boat. We used 50-pound fluoro leaders, small hooks buried in the chunk, no weight, just let it flutter down naturally. Landed four more yellowfin that night, one right at 70 pounds, and had a big fish — bigeye-sized run, heavy and slow — that pulled hook after ten minutes of stalemate. That's canyon chunking. You win some, you lose some, and the ones you lose stick with you longer than the ones you land.

The real story of the week, though, was the white marlin. We had one come up on the left long rigger Thursday, ate a ballyhoo clean, and we actually got the flag up — first white of the season for us. Talked to a few other crews working the Wilmington and Baltimore both, and they're seeing the same thing: scattered white marlin showing on the troll, not stacked yet, but building. That lines up with what we expected out of this month — the billfish migration typically starts trickling through the mid-Atlantic canyons in mid-to-late July, and this looks like the front edge of it. If you want a shot at marlin right now, keep naked ballyhoo or small skirted baits in the pattern along with your tuna spread. Don't rig the whole boat for tuna and be surprised when a white eats your teaser bait.

Wahoo have been quiet for us — we marked a couple of high-speed strikes on the wire but nothing stuck, and I haven't heard much wahoo talk out of Washington Canyon either. Bluefin are still mostly an inshore story right now, schoolies working bait balls closer to the 30-fathom line, which isn't really our program out here on the canyon edge.

Water's been running warm and stable, that eddy hasn't slid off the wall the way they sometimes do mid-week, and as long as it holds through the weekend I'd expect the same general pattern — troll mornings on the temp break, switch to the chunk after 6 p.m. if the current's right. The Canyon Challenge wraps up this weekend and from what I'm hearing at the dock, boats have found enough fish to make it a real tournament, not a coin-flip. If the eddy stays put, I'd run the same corner of the Wilmington Monday and Tuesday before the wind forecast for midweek potentially stirs things up. If it slides east like these things sometimes do, I'd shift effort toward the Baltimore's north edge and start the search over. Either way, this was a week where making the shorter, smarter run paid off — sometimes the math on fuel and time matters more than the rumor on the radio.
